dump.name: gtfo-inspection/dumper/dump.cs
dump.note: Local read-only copy used for this audit. dump.cs records the short type name, the il2cpp RVA, the vtable Slot for every virtual/override and the exact parameter list.

method: Read-only static analysis. No assembly is loaded into the CLR, no game process is started, nothing is written to a profile or to the game directory.
A method body begins at its dump.cs RVA, is bounded by the next distinct RVA of the same owning type (cap 0x4000 bytes) and stops at the first terminator followed by int3/nop padding.

The body is decoded with Iced x64. An edge below is a literal E8/E9 rel32 call at that site. Indirect dispatch (vtable call, delegate Invoke, register) is NOT resolved, so a method with no listed caller is normally called through one of those and is not dead code.

rvaSharing is the number of dump.cs method entries that declare that exact RVA in the whole image. share=1 means the RVA identifies exactly one method entry anywhere in the dump, which is what a Harmony patch target needs.

A dump.cs method entry carries a Slot number exactly when it is declared virtual, override or abstract in the shipped metadata; dump.cs contains zero virtual/override/abstract entries without a Slot. So isVirtual below is read from the presence of Slot, not guessed.

Every call site is reported with a [loop] or [straight] marker: [loop] means the call instruction sits inside a backward-branch region of the same body, so one instruction there runs once per iteration.

Entry and caller signatures are written as namespace-qualified dump names, which are the exact il2cpp type names; the parameter list of each entry comes from its dump.cs declaration line. Callee signatures in the calls lists are resolved from the dump.cs RVA index, so they name the method that lives at that RVA rather than restating a prototype string.

answer.question: Where does a shot enter the game, where is a bullet hit decided, how is the shooting player obtained, and how does a client shot reach the host?
conclusion: One entry point per weapon family, and every one of them is the same virtual slot: Fire(bool resetRecoilSimilarity) is Slot 151 on BulletWeapon, BulletWeaponSynced, Shotgun and ShotgunSynced. There is no separate OnShot/OnFire entry in this build.

BulletWeapon.Fire is the unsynced body (third-person / bot / AI holder), BulletWeaponSynced.Fire overrides it and is the body that reads the shooting player; Shotgun and ShotgunSynced override Fire only to add the spread loop.

Every Fire body reaches the single static hit routine BulletWeapon.BulletHit exactly through direct call sites; BulletHit is the only place that turns a ray into a hit, so it is the single fact a hit-based behaviour should be driven from.

The ray struct that BulletHit receives carries a PlayerAgent field: Weapon.WeaponHitData.owner at offset 0x68, and the struct is constructed inside every Fire body (Weapon.WeaponHitData::ctor). Every Fire body also reads PlayerAgent.get_Owner, which returns SNet_Player (the agent's network identity); whether the Fire body writes a PlayerAgent into the owner field is not visible in this metadata and is listed under unverified.

Fire is virtual with no direct caller anywhere in the image: it is invoked through the wielding item's vtable, so the only stable interception point for 'a shot happened' is Fire itself (or the hit routine), not any caller.

A shot produces MULTIPLE BulletHit calls, not one: BulletWeapon.Fire and BulletWeaponSynced.Fire each contain two BulletHit call sites (one straight-line, one inside a loop) and Shotgun.Fire / ShotgunSynced.Fire contain one that sits inside the pellet/spread loop. Fire, not BulletHit, is therefore the only per-shot event.

The client-side replication entry OnSyncFire(int shots) exists on BulletWeaponSynced (override of the Slot 128 virtual declared by ItemEquippable) and is 28 bytes long with only an unconditional branch: it forwards to the private OnSyncFireRegular / OnSyncFireBurst helpers. OnSyncFire does not call BulletHit and does not call Fire.
consequences: One shot publishes one fact: publish from the Fire entry (or from a per-Fire scope opened there and closed after the last hit), never from BulletHit.

If a per-hit fact is genuinely required, the identity of the shot must be carried by the caller of Fire, because BulletHit receives only the ray struct and a damageSearchID parameter (uint, default 0) that is passed in from Fire.

methods.name: Fire
methods.dumpSignature: public virtual void Fire(bool resetRecoilSimilarity = True)
methods.reason: The only Fire body that is not synced and not a shotgun/spread override; it is the Slot 151 implementation reached when the wielded item is the unsynced weapon.

methods.name: Fire
methods.dumpSignature: public override void Fire(bool resetRecoilSimilarity = True)
methods.reason: Override of the same Slot 151 on the synced weapon; it is the Fire body that reads PlayerAgent.get_Owner directly and the one that decides the whiz-by behaviour, so it is the natural per-shot host hook.

methods.name: Fire
methods.dumpSignature: public override void Fire(bool resetRecoilSimilarity = True)
methods.reason: Both BulletHit call sites sit inside loop regions, which is the spread/pellet loop; a single trigger pull therefore produces many hits.

methods.name: Fire
methods.dumpSignature: public override void Fire(bool resetRecoilSimilarity = True)
methods.reason: Synced shotgun override; one hit call site, inside the spread loop.

methods.name: BulletHit
methods.dumpSignature: public static bool BulletHit(Weapon.WeaponHitData weaponRayData, bool doDamage, float additionalDis = 0, uint damageSearchID = 0, bool allowDirectionalBonus = True)
methods.reason: Static and non-virtual, so every caller is a literal call site and the list above is the complete set of weapon Fire bodies that can produce a bullet hit. It takes the ray data by value, so a caller cannot be recovered from a patch on this method.

methods.name: CastWeaponRay
methods.dumpSignature: public static bool CastWeaponRay(Transform muzzle, ref Weapon.WeaponHitData weaponRayData, int altRayCastMask = -1)
methods.reason: Same overload is a thin forwarder; both synced Fire bodies reach the ray cast through it, and it is where the WeaponHitData is normally created and filled.

methods.name: CastWeaponRay
methods.dumpSignature: public static bool CastWeaponRay(Transform alignTransform, ref Weapon.WeaponHitData weaponRayData, Vector3 originPos, int altRayCastMask = -1)
methods.reason: The real ray cast that fills the WeaponHitData used by BulletHit. It is not a per-shot event by itself, because the shotgun and the loop branch call it more than once per Fire.

methods.name: OnSyncFire
methods.reason: Overrides the Slot 128 virtual declared on Gear.ItemEquippable; the 28-byte body only forwards to the private OnSyncFireRegular and OnSyncFireBurst helpers, and it is reached through the item vtable, so the replication caller has no literal call site.

methods.name: OnSyncFireRegular
methods.reason: Empty body; the sync entry does not itself fire or damage.

methods.name: OnSyncFire
methods.reason: This RVA is the shared empty stub used by 2102 different method entries, so it must never be used as a Harmony patch target; it is listed only to show the slot the synced weapon overrides.

methods.name: owner-field
methods.reason: Field offset 0x68 of the by-value struct that BulletHit receives. This is the game's own owner slot on the ray data; the naming is the game's, the assignment is not verified here.

dedupe.question: Where can one shot publish exactly one fact when a single shot produces several hits?
dedupe.answer: At Fire, the Slot 151 entry that every weapon family overrides, and never at BulletWeapon.BulletHit.
grounds: Fire is called once per trigger pull per weapon instance; BulletHit is called once per ray, and the shotgun and the loop branches call it repeatedly inside one Fire body (see the [loop] call sites above).
Fire is virtual and has no literal caller, so a postfix on the Slot 151 method catches every path that can start a shot without touching the caller chain.
BulletHit is static and takes the ray struct by value, so a postfix there cannot tell which weapon, which shot, or which trigger pull the hit belongs to.

options.shape: Postfix on Gear.BulletWeapon::Fire / Gear.BulletWeaponSynced::Fire / Gear.Shotgun::Fire / Gear.ShotgunSynced::Fire at Slot 151.
options.publishes: exactly one shot fact per Fire call
options.note: Four separate RVAs are needed because each family overrides Fire; a single Harmony patch on the base body does not cover the overrides.

options.shape: Postfix on Gear.BulletWeaponSynced::Fire and Gear.ShotgunSynced::Fire only.
options.publishes: one shot fact per shot made with a player-wielded synced weapon
options.note: Covers the player path and skips bots and unsynced holders, which is the narrower choice if bot shots must not count.

options.shape: Prefix on Fire opens a per-shot scope and stores a token; postfix on BulletHit reports one hit per ray and closes the scope.
options.publishes: one shot fact plus the individual hits of that shot
options.note: Requires a scope owned by the patch, because BulletHit carries no shot identity of its own; this mirrors the runtime lease shape the framework already uses for other domains.

notRecommended.reason: The Slot 128 base body is the shared empty stub at RVA 0x353190 with 2102 method entries on the same RVA, and the synced override only forwards to two empty helpers, so it cannot represent a shot.
One shot calls the ray cast once per pellet and once per loop iteration, so the count is not one per shot.

unverified.statement: That Weapon.WeaponHitData.owner is written with the shooting agent before BulletHit reads it.
unverified.reason: The dump gives the field, the offset and the fact that every Fire body constructs the struct and reads PlayerAgent.get_Owner, but the assignment statements are not present in the metadata; the interop assemblies are runtime-invoke thunks, so they carry no body either.
unverified.whatWouldSettleIt: A decompilation of the Fire bodies (il2cpp metadata plus the native image), or a runtime postfix on Weapon.WeaponHitData::.ctor that logs the struct.

unverified.statement: Whether a client's trigger pull makes the host run Fire (and therefore BulletHit) for that client.
unverified.reason: Fire is virtual with no literal caller, and the replication caller is resolved through the item vtable, which the decoder deliberately does not follow. OnSyncFire on the synced weapon is reached the same way and its body does not call Fire, so the static evidence here shows the client-side reception entry but not the host-side re-execution.
unverified.whatWouldSettleIt: A runtime trace (Harmony postfix logging) on the host while a client fires, or a full vtable-aware decompilation of the weapon replication callbacks.

unverified.statement: Whether bots and AI holders run the unsynced Fire body or a third-person body.
unverified.reason: The unsynced Fire bodies are the only ones the decoder sees as containing BulletHit, but which holder wields them is a runtime object-graph fact.
unverified.see: enemydmgev for the damage side; the holder question is out of scope here.

unverified.statement: What BulletHit does once it has a hit, and how the damage reaches the target.
unverified.reason: The damage entry point and the receiving side belong to the damage domain.

unverified.statement: RifleWeaponSynced only overrides PlayRecoilAnim (Slot 153, RVA 0x13C2420), so the rifle reuses the BulletWeaponSynced bodies.
unverified.reason: Verified from the dump declaration list; listed as a note rather than a wired hook.

limits: No claim about runtime behaviour: nothing here was executed, and a literal call edge only proves that a call site exists in the shipped binary.
rvaSharing counts duplicate method entries in the local dump.cs; a value of 1 is necessary for a safe patch target but does not prove that the RVA is not reached through a shared jump target.

The decoder bounds a body by the next distinct RVA of the same owning type. If the image stores a method out of line from its type, the bound can be shorter than the real body, which would under-report call sites, never invent them.
The [loop] marker is a backward-branch region test inside one body. It proves that a call instruction can run more than once per entry, and it does not measure how many times it actually runs.
